results.result: High-frequency optogenetic activation of layer II/III pyramidal cells induces frequency-dependent vasoconstriction in cortical slices. Photostimulation at 1-5 Hz failed to elicit reliable vascular responses, while 10 Hz induced vasoconstriction in 4 of 5 arterioles (AUC = -1.7 ± 1.1 x 10³ %.s), and 20 Hz induced vasoconstriction in all arterioles (AUC = -3.7 ± 0.7 x 10³ %.s, n=10). The vasoconstriction magnitude at 20 Hz was statistically different from lower frequencies (p<0.05 vs 1, 2, and 5 Hz).
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C69 and C76 provide converging evidence from electrophysiological recordings (C52-C56), vascular imaging (C57-C66), and statistical analyses (C67-C69) demonstrating frequency-dependent vasoconstriction. The data show clear dose-response relationships with appropriate controls (wild-type mice, C75) and exclusion of confounds (cortical spreading depression, C70-C73). Sample sizes are adequate (n=4-10 arterioles per condition) with statistical significance reported.

results.result: Optogenetic stimulation induces a frequency-dependent increase in pyramidal cell somatic Ca²⁺ that precedes vasoconstriction. The Ca²⁺ response at 20 Hz (ΔF/F0 = 79.5 ± 17.7%, n=9 cells) was more than twice that at 2 Hz (ΔF/F0 = 34.5 ± 3.7%, n=9 cells; p=0.024), while the number of evoked spikes was approximately five times higher.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C84 demonstrate a clear correlation between stimulation frequency, Ca²⁺ elevation, and spike number using combined electrophysiology and calcium imaging (Figure 2). The statistical comparison is appropriate (t-test, p=0.024), and the temporal relationship (Ca²⁺ increase precedes vasoconstriction) is established. However, the claim that Ca²⁺ increase "precedes" vasoconstriction could be more rigorously demonstrated with simultaneous measurements.

results.result: Pyramidal cell-induced vasoconstriction requires action potential firing and partially involves glutamatergic transmission. TTX (1 µM) completely abolished vasoconstriction (AUC = 0.4 ± 0.4 x 10³ %.s, n=6, p<0.001), while glutamate receptor antagonists reduced vasoconstriction magnitude by approximately half (AUC = -1.6 ± 0.4 x 10³ %.s, p=0.016).
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C94 provide strong pharmacological evidence with appropriate controls. TTX experiments (C86-C88) definitively establish AP-dependence, while glutamate receptor antagonist experiments (C92-C93) demonstrate partial involvement. The ~50% reduction with glutamate antagonists suggests additional mechanisms, which is appropriately acknowledged (C94). Statistical tests are appropriate with significant p-values.

results.result: Prostaglandins derived mainly from COX-2 activity mediate pyramidal cell-induced vasoconstriction both ex vivo and in vivo. Ex vivo, indomethacin (5 µM) completely abolished vasoconstriction (AUC = 0.0 ± 0.2 x 10³ %.s, n=10, p<0.001). In vivo, indomethacin reversed the constriction phase (AUCCtrl = -291.5 ± 92.4 %.s vs AUCIndo = 332.4 ± 184.4 %.s, p=0.016). COX-2 inhibitor NS-398 was more potent than COX-1 inhibitor SC-560.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C125 provide robust evidence across both ex vivo and in vivo preparations with appropriate pharmacological controls. The complete abolition by indomethacin and NS-398, combined with partial reduction by SC-560, supports the predominant role of COX-2. The in vivo validation (C117-C120) strengthens the ex vivo findings. Statistical analyses are appropriate with significant p-values. Sample sizes are adequate (n=7-10).

results.result: PGE2-induced vasoconstriction primarily acts through EP1 receptors and, to a lesser extent, EP3 receptors. EP1 antagonist ONO-8130 reduced vasoconstriction (AUC = 0.3 ± 0.3 x 10³ %.s, p<0.001), while EP3 antagonist L-798,106 had a lesser effect (AUC = -0.9 ± 0.4 x 10³ %.s, p<0.001). Exogenous PGE2 induced dose-dependent vasoconstriction that persisted after removal and was independent of AP firing.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C140 provide comprehensive pharmacological evidence for PGE2 receptor involvement. The differential effects of EP1 vs EP3 antagonists are well-documented with appropriate statistics. Exogenous PGE2 experiments (C136-C138) support direct vascular effects. The FP receptor antagonist AL-8810 showed a trend but did not reach significance (C130-C131, p=0.053), which is appropriately reported. The claim about AP-independence (C140) is supported by TTX experiments with exogenous PGE2.

results.result: Subpopulations of layer II-III pyramidal cells express the molecular machinery for cell-autonomous PGE2 and PGF2α synthesis. Single-cell RT-PCR revealed that COX-1 (25%, n=4/16) and COX-2 (31%, n=5/16) were never co-expressed. Most cells expressed cPGES (88%, n=14/16), and all COX-2 positive neurons co-expressed both PGES and PGFS. Approximately half of pyramidal cells express all transcripts necessary for PGE2 and PGF2α synthesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C114 provide detailed molecular characterization using single-cell RT-PCR (n=16 cells). The mutually exclusive expression of COX-1 and COX-2 (C100) is clearly demonstrated. The high detection rate of PGES enzymes and systematic co-expression patterns support the conclusion about cell-autonomous synthesis capacity. However, the sample size (n=16) is modest, and protein-level validation would strengthen these mRNA-based findings.

results.result: Neurogenic vasoconstriction involves NPY-releasing interneurons acting on Y1 receptors and astrocytes via 20-HETE, but not via K+ release through BK channels. Y1 receptor antagonist BIBP3226 abolished vasoconstriction (AUC = -0.3 ± 0.2 x 10³ %.s, p<0.001), while CYP450 ω-hydroxylase inhibitor HET-0016 reduced it (AUC = -1.6 ± 0.7 x 10³ %.s, p=0.016). BK channel blocker paxilline had no effect (AUC = -3.7 ± 0.3 x 10³ %.s, p=1).
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C151 provide clear pharmacological evidence for intermediary cell involvement. The complete abolition by BIBP3226 (C148-C149) demonstrates critical NPY/Y1 involvement, while partial reduction by HET-0016 (C145-C146) supports astrocytic 20-HETE contribution. The lack of effect with paxilline (C143-C144) appropriately rules out BK channel involvement. Statistical analyses are sound with adequate sample sizes (n=10 per condition).

results.result: The Emx1-cre;Ai32 transgenic mouse model expresses ChR2H134R in cortical glutamatergic neurons, conferring robust pyramidal cell photoexcitability. Control experiments in wild-type mice lacking ChR2 showed no vascular response to 20 Hz photostimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C51 and C75 establish the validity of the optogenetic model with appropriate citations and negative controls. The wild-type control (C75) rules out light-induced artifacts. However, the manuscript could benefit from quantification of ChR2 expression levels and spatial distribution beyond the qualitative description.

results.result: The observed vasoconstriction is not due to cortical spreading depression. The rate of change in light transmittance associated with cell swelling remained below the threshold for cortical spreading depression (all <2 %.s⁻¹).
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C73 appropriately address a potential confound. The quantitative criterion (dΔT/dt <2 %.s⁻¹) based on Zhou et al., 2010 is clearly stated and data are provided in Table 1. This control strengthens the interpretation that vasoconstriction is a direct consequence of pyramidal cell activity rather than spreading depression.

results.result: Background claims establish that neurovascular coupling links neuronal activity to cerebral blood flow and is essential for brain function. While vasodilation mechanisms are well-documented, vasoconstriction mechanisms remain less understood.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 and C13-C18 provide appropriate context from established literature with proper citations. These background claims accurately characterize the state of the field and motivate the study's focus on vasoconstriction mechanisms. The citations are appropriate and support the statements made.

results.result: Prior work demonstrates that the correlation between neuronal activity and cerebral blood flow is not always maintained, including cases where vasodilation occurs without substantial neuronal response, neuronal activity occurs without increased hemodynamics, and pathological conditions show vasoconstriction with intense activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C23 accurately summarize prior literature with appropriate citations. These claims establish the complexity of neurovascular coupling and provide context for the current findings. The citations support the statements, though the authors should verify that they accurately represent the cited work.

results.result: Methodological considerations establish that ex vivo brain slices provide controlled environments for pharmacological studies but lack connectivity and blood flow, requiring in vivo validation. Chronic anesthetized animals provide a valuable model for validation despite reduced network activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C37 appropriately discuss the strengths and limitations of different experimental approaches. The acknowledgment of ex vivo limitations (C30-C31) and the rationale for using anesthetized animals for validation (C35-C37) demonstrate methodological rigor. The citation to Rungta et al., 2021 supports the claim about slowed but preserved NVC in anesthetized animals.

results.result: Prior work has identified multiple vasodilatory messengers but fewer vasoconstrictor mechanisms. GABAergic interneurons releasing NPY and astrocytes via 20-HETE or K+ are known vasoconstrictors, but pyramidal cell involvement has been overlooked.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C43 accurately characterize prior knowledge with appropriate citations. The statement that pyramidal cell involvement has been overlooked (C43) is supported by the literature review and motivates the current study. However, the authors should verify that no prior studies have examined pyramidal cell-mediated vasoconstriction.

results.result: PGE2 is a bimodal messenger that can induce either vasodilation or vasoconstriction depending on concentration and site of action. Under physiological conditions, PGE2 is produced by astrocytes (via COX-1) or pyramidal cells (via COX-2). The hypothesis is proposed that pyramidal cells may be responsible for vasoconstriction when spiking activity is high.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C49 provide appropriate background with citations supporting the bimodal nature of PGE2 and its cellular sources. The hypothesis (C49) is clearly stated as speculation based on prior work. This sets up the experimental investigation that follows. The citations appropriately support the background claims.

results.result: Background on vasoactive substance release establishes that vasodilatory substance synthesis/release requires intracellular Ca²⁺ elevation, but little is known about vasoconstrictor release. Action potentials in pyramidal cells induce both somatic Ca²⁺ elevation and glutamate release.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78 and C85 provide appropriate background with citations (Attwell et al., 2010; Cauli and Hamel, 2010; Smetters et al., 1999). These claims establish the rationale for examining Ca²⁺ dynamics and glutamate involvement. The characterization of the knowledge gap (C78) is appropriate.

results.result: Potential mechanisms are proposed whereby high glutamate levels from pyramidal cells may activate NPY interneurons or astrocytes through ionotropic/metabotropic receptors, or directly activate NMDA receptors on smooth muscle cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C91 are speculative hypotheses supported by citations but not directly tested in this study. While the citations support these possibilities, the claims are presented as potential mechanisms rather than demonstrated findings. The subsequent experiments (C92-C93) show glutamate involvement but don't definitively establish which of these mechanisms operates.

results.result: PGE2 released by pyramidal cells can activate astrocytes and neurons, which express PGE2 receptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C142 are supported by appropriate citations (Clasadonte et al., 2011; Di Cesare et al., 2006; Tasic et al., 2016; Zeisel et al., 2015). These claims provide context for the indirect mechanisms examined in the study. The citations appropriately support the receptor expression patterns.

results.result: Summary conclusions establish that pyramidal cell activity leads to arteriolar vasoconstriction in a frequency-dependent manner correlating with Ca²⁺ increase. The response involves PGE2 from COX-2 pyramidal cells acting on EP1/EP3 receptors, with intermediary roles for NPY interneurons and astrocytes via 20-HETE.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C158 appropriately summarize the major findings supported by the experimental data. These conclusions are well-supported by the grouped results above. The summary accurately reflects the relative contributions of different mechanisms (PGE2 as primary, NPY and 20-HETE as intermediary).

results.result: Optogenetic stimulation of layer II/III pyramidal cells at 10-20 Hz induces frequency-dependent vasoconstriction in cortical slices. The vasoconstriction magnitude correlates with photostimulation frequency, with 20 Hz producing the strongest and most rapid response (AUC = −3.7 ± 0.7 x 10³ %.s), while 1-5 Hz failed to elicit reliable fast vascular responses.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge this finding, with one stating 'the authors show that strong optogenetic stimulation of cortical pyramidal neurons is leading to constriction' and noting '10-s optogenetic stimulation at 10 and 20 Hz leads to vasoconstriction (Figure 1).' The data are described as 'convincing' and the mechanism is characterized as an 'important finding.'

results.result: Photostimulation induces a frequency-dependent increase in pyramidal cell somatic Ca2+ that precedes vasoconstriction. The Ca2+ response at 20 Hz (ΔF/F0=79.5 ± 17.7%) was more than twice that at 2 Hz (ΔF/F0=34.5 ± 3.7%), correlating with approximately five times more evoked spikes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly note this finding, stating the study shows vasoconstriction 'in line with a stimulation frequency-dependent increase in somatic calcium (Figure 2).' The correlation between firing frequency and calcium increase is accepted as part of the mechanistic evidence.

results.result: Vasoconstriction requires action potential firing and partially involves glutamatergic transmission. TTX completely abolished the vasoconstriction (AUC = 0.4 ± 0.4 x 10³ %.s), while glutamate receptor antagonists reduced it by approximately half (AUC = −1.6±0.4 x 10³ %.s).
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge this result, noting 'the vascular effects were abolished in presence in TTX and significantly reduced in presence of glutamate receptor antagonists (Figure 3).' The data are described as supporting the authors' conclusions about the mechanism.

results.result: Single-cell RT-PCR reveals that approximately 50% of layer II/III pyramidal cells express enzymes necessary for PGE2 and PGF2α synthesis. COX-1 was detected in 25% and COX-2 in 31% of pyramidal cells (never co-expressed), while cPGES was observed in 88% of cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly note this finding, stating 'the authors further show with RT-PCR on RNA isolated from patched cells that ~50% of analyzed cells express COX-1 or -2 and other enzymes required to produce PGE2 or PGF2a (Figure 4).' One reviewer confirms 'Single-cell RT-PCR from patched neurons confirmed the presence of the PGE2 synthesis pathway.'

results.result: Prostaglandins derived mainly from COX-2 activity mediate pyramidal cell-induced vasoconstriction. The non-selective COX inhibitor indomethacin completely abolished the response ex vivo (AUC = 0.0 ± 0.2 x 10³ %.s), as did the COX-2 inhibitor NS-398 (AUC = 0.1 ± 0.3 x 10³ %.s), while the COX-1 inhibitor SC-560 reduced it (AUC = −1.4±0.7 x 10³ %.s).
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge this finding, noting 'blockade of COX-1 and -2 (indomethacin), or COX-2 (NS-398) abolishes constriction' and that the study demonstrates vasoconstriction 'is mediated through the cyclooxygenase-2 / prostaglandin E2 / EP1 and EP3 receptor pathway.' The data are described as 'convincing.'

results.result: In vivo validation in anesthetized mice shows that 10 Hz photostimulation induces biphasic vascular response: initial vasodilation followed by sustained vasoconstriction. The constriction phase was inhibited by intravenous indomethacin (AUCCtrl = -291.5 ± 92.4 %.s vs. AUCIndo = 332.4 ± 184.4 %.s).
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly note this validation, stating 'In animals with chronic cranial window that were anesthetized with ketamine and medetomidine, 10-s long optogenetic stimulation at 10 Hz leads to considerable constriction, which is reduced in presence of indomethacin.' The in vivo data are recognized as important validation of the ex vivo findings.

results.result: PGE2-induced vasoconstriction primarily acts through EP1 receptors and to a lesser extent EP3 receptors. The EP1 antagonist ONO-8130 reduced vasoconstriction magnitude (AUC = 0.3±0.3 x 10³ %.s), while the EP3 antagonist L-798,106 had a lesser effect (AUC = −0.9±0.4 x 10³ %.s).
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge this finding, noting 'blockade of EP1 and EP3 showed the same effect ex vivo' and that the mechanism involves 'activation of arteriolar EP1 and EP3 receptors.' The receptor specificity is accepted as part of the PGE2 pathway characterization.

results.result: Astrocytes partially mediate vasoconstriction via 20-HETE but not via K+ release. Selective inhibition of CYP450 ω-hydroxylase with HET-0016 reduced vasoconstriction magnitude (AUC = −1.6 ± 0.7 x 10³ %.s), while BK channel blockade with paxilline had no effect.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly note this finding, stating the study shows 'contribution of NPY-releasing interneurons and astrocytes releasing 20-HETE' and that 'blockade of 20-HETE synthesis caused moderate...reduction of constriction.' The astrocyte contribution is recognized as part of the overall mechanism.

results.result: NPY-releasing interneurons contribute to vasoconstriction through Y1 receptor activation. Antagonism of NPY Y1 receptors by BIBP3226 abolished neurogenic vasoconstriction (AUC = −0.3 ± 0.2 x 10³ %.s).
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledge the finding ('blockade of...NPY Y1 receptor [caused] a complete reduction of constriction'), one reviewer raises a critical concern: 'how is the complete inhibition of the constriction by the NPY Y1 receptor antagonist BIBP3226 consistent with a direct effect of PGE2 and 20-HETE in arterioles?' This logical inconsistency suggests uncertainty about the interpretation of NPY's role relative to the direct PGE2 pathway.

results.result: Control experiments rule out cortical spreading depression and ChR2-independent light effects. The rate of light transmittance change remained below that of cortical spreading depression, and 20 Hz photostimulation did not induce vascular responses in wild-type mice lacking ChR2.
results.evaluation: While not explicitly discussed by reviewers, these control experiments address potential confounds that reviewers might have raised. The absence of reviewer concerns about these alternative explanations suggests implicit acceptance of these controls as adequate.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement. Both evaluations find the frequency-dependent vasoconstriction data convincing and supported, covering identical claim sets (C6-C8, C52-C69, C76). Both note the quality of electrophysiological and vascular imaging evidence with appropriate controls.

Complete agreement. Both evaluations support the correlation between stimulation frequency, calcium elevation, and vasoconstriction (C79-C84). Both accept the mechanistic link demonstrated in Figure 2.

Full agreement. Both evaluations find the TTX and glutamate receptor antagonist experiments (C86-C88, C92-C94) convincing and well-controlled, supporting action potential dependence and partial glutamate involvement.

Complete agreement. Both evaluations support the single-cell RT-PCR findings (C98-C114) demonstrating COX-1/COX-2 expression and PGE2 synthesis pathway components in pyramidal neurons. Both acknowledge the molecular characterization as convincing.

Strong agreement on COX inhibitor effects (C115-C116, C121-C125). Both find the pharmacological evidence for COX-2/PGE2 pathway convincing. OpenEval additionally covers in vivo validation claims (C117-C120) that peer reviewers address separately.

Agreement on in vivo validation. Both evaluations support the in vivo indomethacin experiments (C117-C120) as important validation of ex vivo findings. Peer reviewers explicitly note this strengthens the conclusions.

Agreement on EP receptor involvement. Both evaluations support the EP1 and EP3 receptor antagonist data (C126-C129, C134-C135). OpenEval covers additional claims about exogenous PGE2 and FP receptors not explicitly discussed by peer reviewers.

Agreement on astrocyte/20-HETE contribution. Both evaluations support the HET-0016 experiments (C145-C147) showing moderate reduction with 20-HETE synthesis blockade, accepting astrocyte involvement as part of the mechanism.

Divergence on NPY/Y1 receptor role. OpenEval finds BIBP3226 data (C148-C150) clearly supported and consistent with intermediary cell involvement. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, raising concern about logical inconsistency between complete NPY inhibition and claimed direct PGE2 effects.

Agreement on control experiments. Both evaluations support the cortical spreading depression exclusion criteria (C70-C73) and wild-type controls (C75). Peer reviewers implicitly accept these controls by not raising concerns.
